records.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
records.summary:
A scattered South Atlantic territory of three island groups that legislated equality island by island: the 2009 constitutional order imposed by the administering state bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation across all three, and equal age of consent sits at 16. Marriage equality arrived in staggered fashion — the first dependency's council approved the ordinance 5-0 in May 2016 and it commenced January 2017, the most remote island followed in August 2017, and the principal island itself completed the set on 20 December 2017 — with adoption law following the same year.

The earlier profile undersold all of this as 'decriminalised' and added an unsourced 'church-conservative' gloss; neither survives the evidence. What is documented is a fast, orderly rights rollout across very small councils, and a total absence of survey data on social attitudes — remoteness, not resistance, is the characterised condition.

sources.claim: Alchetron (Wikipedia-derived): LGBT rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - same-sex activity legal; the 2009 Constitution Order bans sexual-orientation discrimination; same-sex marriage legal on Ascension since 1 Jan 2017, with Tristan da Cunha following; Saint Helena did not then recognise same-sex unions.

GayLawNet laws page for Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha: equal age of consent at 16; the 2009 Constitution Order Section 5 guarantees fundamental rights 'without distinction of any kind, such as sex, sexual orientation...'; territory-level legal references.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror, redirects to the territory article): LGBTQ rights on Ascension Island - the marriage ordinance approved 31 May 2016 (5-0), signed and gazetted 20 June, commenced 1 January 2017.

records.name: Solomon Islands
records.summary: Solomon Islands is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years); no LGR; documented social hostility; weak state capacity post-Tensions; no open community infrastructure.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Solomon Islands: documents the legal status — same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era law, up to 14 years.

NOTE: Only the Human Dignity Trust homepage was retrievable at fetch time (no Solomon Islands-specific page); the Trust maps jurisdictions criminalising LGBT people, which include the Solomon Islands.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: no security-force abuses; violence and discrimination against women prevalent; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents lengthy pretrial detention, corruption, violence against women - general context; no LGBT-specific abuses reported.
US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Solomon Islands: documents the RAMSI assistance mission, the Lusibaea case, and general human-rights conditions - baseline assessment.

SIBC (June 2018): Governor General Sir Frank Kabui warned Solomon Islands about same-sex marriage in his Queen's birthday speech - 'Same sex marriage cannot populate the world'; noted sections 160, 161 and 162 of the Penal Code are 'the relevant prohibitions against same sex marriage and associated conduct' and challenged the country to 'remain steadfast against this onslaught'.

records.name: Sierra Leone
records.summary: Sierra Leone is dangerous for trans visitors. The 1861 Offences Against the Person Act criminalises buggery with up to life imprisonment (men only) — enforcement is limited but discrimination and violence are regular; no LGR; a small community organises quietly.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sierra Leone's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act).

Amnesty International Sierra Leone report 2025: freedom of expression threatened through cybersecurity libel provisions; new legislation protected women's and girls' rights but failed to criminalise FGM; general human-rights context, not trans-specific.

Joint ICCPR shadow report (March 2014) to the UN Human Rights Committee: 'Breaking the Silence on Human Rights Violations in Sierra Leone' - discrimination and violence based on SOGI; covers civil-war sexual violence, discrimination in health and education, hate speech by religious institutions, and hate crimes against LGBTI human-rights defenders.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Sierra Leone: documents police killings, corruption, FGM/C, and 'official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals'.

GlobalGayz archive of Sierra Leone news and reports: the rape and murder of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy (2004), her killer's escape, the government MSM study, and homophobic reactions to interviews - the Hirschfeld-Eddy Foundation is named partly in her memory.

records.name: El Salvador
records.summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception with mass arbitrary detention (75,000+ imprisoned, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

sources.claim: Foreign Policy (Mar 2020): 'Transgender Asylum-Seeker's Death Could Prompt El Salvador's First Hate Crime Homicide Conviction' — a landmark case on anti-trans violence in the justice system.
NOTE: This InSight Crime article is about Latin America's homicide rates generally, not El Salvador's LGBT situation specifically; included as general security context.

Academic article (Dilemas, 2024): 'Denied deaths: Profile of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador (2000-2020)' - builds a profile of crimes, victims and perpetrators of anti-LGBTI+ homicides in El Salvador over two decades.

HRW report (Oct 2020) 'Every Day I Live in Fear': violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras, and obstacles to US asylum - opens with the story of Camila Díaz Córdova, a 29-year-old trans woman who fled El Salvador and was later killed there.

HRW report (Jan 2021) 'I'm Lucky to Still Be Alive': violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador - full report with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries.

HRW (July 2020): 'El Salvador: Police Officers Convicted in Transgender Murder' - three police officers convicted for the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a rare case of accountability for anti-trans violence.
Washington Blade (Sept 2015): El Salvador lawmakers approved enhanced hate-crime penalties covering crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity.

records.name: San Marino
records.summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. ILGA-Europe lists San Marino among states with no functioning legal gender recognition process (resident-facing gap only). There is no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, tourism-dependent republic surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map legal gender recognition category page (2026): San Marino is listed among countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition; self-determination-based recognition exists in 12 countries (Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malta, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland).

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 - Legal Gender Recognition chapter: country-by-country findings for 2025, including Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at UPR, trans activist Luana Myrto's legal action in Albania, Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree, and other European developments.

ILGA compilation of SOGIESC recommendations from the 34th UPR Working Group session (Nov 2019) - includes San Marino's review among 12 countries examined; documents the SOGIESC recommendations each state received and accepted.
Euronews (June 2019): San Marino banned discrimination based on sexual orientation (page largely navigation content at fetch time).
The Guardian (April 2022): San Marino appointed the world's first openly gay head of state - Paolo Rondelli named one of two captains regent in 'a country making strides on gay rights'.
Euronews Italian (Nov 2018, in Italian): San Marino approved a civil-unions law, leaner than Italy's Cirinnà law - the legislative milestone for relationship recognition.

records.name: Somalia
records.summary:
Somalia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Somalia's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code; death penalty under Sharia in some regions).

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); al-Shabaab enforces strict Sharia with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.
US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - continued criminalisation, al-Shabaab executions, and no protections for LGBT persons.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Somalia (archived): documents the conflict, al-Shabaab abuses, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Feb 2016): legal advocate Benjamin Christman's report 'on the Treatment of Gay Persons in Somalia' sustains asylum claims - beyond the 3-year anti-homosexuality law, al-Shabaab's Sharia enforcement may punish homosexuality by death; UN and UK guidance identifies gay persons as a 'risk profile' for return.

Al Jazeera (July 2013): 'Gay Somali refugees face death threats' - gay, lesbian and HIV-infected refugees in Kenya face persecution if returned; Jamal, a Somali journalist: 'Warlords have made Somalia a death chamber for gays and lesbians'; Said Elmi: 'It will be a massacre.'

records.name: Serbia
records.summary:
Serbia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the Interior Ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, a masked attacker smashed the Pride information centre's front in 2025, Pride marches require heavy police protection, and testosterone HRT supply-chain disruptions have been documented.

Serbia is outside the Schengen area (border checks for foreign travellers), legal-gender-recognition reform has stalled (the Law on Gender Identity was not adopted), and the anti-discrimination law is weakly enforced — public institutions "make minimal effort." One mitigating factor is a Belgrade prison's trans-sensitive search policy, which lets trans women choose the search arrangement, though watchdogs flag training gaps.

Serbia has a lesbian prime minister (Ana Brnabić), but stalled legislation and police brutality make that largely symbolic rather than substantive protection. Major-tourist Belgrade is "conditionally" manageable with situational awareness.

sources.claim: BIRN/Balkan Insight (Feb 2024): Serbia investigates allegations of police assault on two LGBT people during a drugs raid on a Belgrade apartment - the Interior Ministry's internal control section referred the complaint (from Da se zna!) to the Prosecutor's Office.

Da se zna! (Sept 2025): presentation of the 8th annual report 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024' - 105 incidents motivated by homophobia and transphobia in 2024, the highest number since monitoring began; includes quantitative and qualitative analyses of hate speech, hate crimes and discrimination.

Association for the Prevention of Torture country page for Serbia: NPM overview (Protector of Citizens as Ombudsman, operational since 2011, cooperating with six CSOs) and links to the Serbia country report on detention safeguards.

HRW World Report 2025 Serbia/Kosovo chapter: intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns in 2024, alongside attacks on journalists and a flawed asylum system (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section).

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Serbia: trans people face testosterone supply shortages (Testosteron Depo); a publication analysed 70 instances of politicians' hate speech (April 2023-April 2024); the Pride Info Centre was attacked in January and announced closure in September after 20+ attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned; a Zoomer survey found three-quarters of trans/non-binary people fear job interviews due to anticipated discrimination.

US State Department 2018 Human Rights Report for Serbia: human-rights issues include government corruption, violence against journalists, and 'crimes including violence targeting Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Intersex (LGBTI) individuals'.

records.name: South Sudan
records.summary:
South Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.

sources.claim: US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for South Sudan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under the 2008 Penal Code (up to 10 years); societal stigma; pervasive conflict-related abuses.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for South Sudan: official assessment - continued criminalisation and societal discrimination; conflict-related violence dominates the human-rights picture.
US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for South Sudan: official assessment - criminalisation, no LGBT-specific protections, and widespread conflict abuses.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for South Sudan: official assessment - criminalisation and societal stigma amid the civil-war aftermath.
US State Department 2018 Human Rights Report for South Sudan: official assessment - criminalisation under the Penal Code and pervasive conflict-related human-rights abuses.
